name: The Birth of Venus
kicker: Botticelli’s Renaissance painting · Venus arrives on shore on a shell
briefing: Sandro Botticelli painted _The Birth of Venus_ in Renaissance Florence, showing the Roman goddess of love arriving on shore, fully grown, standing on a giant scallop shell. The wind god Zephyrus blows her toward land while a goddess of the seasons rushes to cover her with a flowered cloak. It was one of the first large non-religious nude paintings since ancient times, and today it hangs in Florence’s Uffizi Gallery.
answerHtml: The Birth of Venus (prompt on Venus; do not accept “Venus of Urbino” or “Rokeby Venus”)

sample.note: 7 real QBReader tossups for this exact answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This painting’s imagery likely draws on Angelo Poliziano’s poem _Stanze per la Giostra_ and the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite, and it was long linked to a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent in the Medici family. None of its figures cast shadows, giving the whole scene a dreamlike, weightless quality that one art historian said lacked classical balance.
tossups.r: Painted in tempera on canvas rather than wood panel, it is often discussed alongside Botticelli’s other large mythological work, _Primavera_. For 10 points, name this painting in which Zephyrus blows the newborn Roman goddess of love to shore on a shell.

tossups.p: Gold-leaf highlights decorate the orange trees behind a cloaked woman on the right side of this painting, while cattails grow near the water’s edge on the left. A detail from this painting appears on an Italian ten-cent euro coin.
tossups.r: The wind god Zephyrus carries the nymph Chloris as he blows the title figure toward shore on a giant scallop shell. For 10 points, name this Sandro Botticelli painting of a Roman goddess’s birth from the sea.

tossups.p: This painting’s central figure strikes a pose borrowed from ancient “Venus Pudica” sculptures, covering her body with her hands and her own long hair. Critics have noted that her unusually elongated neck and torso owe more to Gothic style than to classical proportion.
tossups.r: An attendant on the right holds out a flowered pink cloak while Zephyrus blows the goddess toward shore. For 10 points, name this Botticelli painting showing the Roman goddess of love arriving on a shell.

tossups.p: This painting hung at the Villa di Castello before moving to its current home, the Uffizi Gallery, in 1815. Painted in tempera on canvas rather than the costlier wood panel typical of the era, it was probably finished in the mid-1480s.
tossups.r: Orange trees with gold-touched leaves fill the background as a robed woman offers a cloak to its central figure. For 10 points, name this painting of a goddess arriving on a shell, by Sandro Botticelli.

tossups.p: The robe-bearing woman on the right of this painting is identified in some accounts as Pomona and in others as a Hora, one of the Greek goddesses of the seasons. She waits in front of an orange grove to cover the painting’s nude central figure.
tossups.r: Zephyrus blows that figure toward shore on a giant scallop shell. For 10 points, name this Sandro Botticelli painting of the Roman goddess of love being born from the sea.

tossups.p: This painting is often discussed alongside Botticelli’s other great mythological canvas, _Primavera_, though the two were likely not created as a pair. Its central figure’s pose recalls ancient statues of a modest, self-covering goddess.
tossups.r: Zephyrus blows the nude figure to shore on a shell while an attendant rushes forward with a pink cloak. For 10 points, name this painting of the birth of the Roman goddess of love, by Sandro Botticelli.

tossups.p: This work is considered one of the first large non-religious nude figures in Western painting since antiquity. Its central figure tries to shield herself with her own flowing hair as she floats ashore.
tossups.r: An attendant offers a flowered cloak while the wind god Zephyrus blows her toward land. For 10 points, name this Botticelli painting of a goddess arriving on a giant shell.

tossups.p: In this painting, the wind god Zephyrus embraces the nymph Chloris as the pair blow its central figure toward the shore. An orange grove with gold-tinted leaves fills the background on the right.
tossups.r: That figure stands nude atop a giant scallop shell, having just been born from sea foam. For 10 points, name this Sandro Botticelli painting of the Roman goddess of love and beauty.

tossups.p: A giant scallop shell carries this painting’s central figure to shore, blown by the wind god Zephyrus. On the right, a woman waits with a flowered pink cloak to cover her.
tossups.r: Sandro Botticelli painted this scene of a Roman goddess’s birth from the sea. For 10 points, name this famous Renaissance painting of the goddess of love.

tossups.p: This painting hangs today in Florence’s Uffizi Gallery, where crowds gather to see its nude central figure standing on a shell. Zephyrus, the god of the west wind, blows her gently toward shore.
tossups.r: Sandro Botticelli painted this scene in Renaissance Florence, probably for a Medici-linked patron. For 10 points, name this painting showing the birth of the Roman goddess of love.

trap.title: Venus: painting or goddess?
trap.body: Some real quiz-bowl tossups ask for “Venus” herself rather than this specific painting — those questions sweep in other famous artworks too, like Titian’s _Venus of Urbino_ and Velázquez’s _Rokeby Venus_, and often accept “Aphrodite” as her Greek name. This painting’s own answer line wants its title, in English or Italian, and never accepts “Aphrodite,” since the question is about one specific canvas, not the goddess in general.
trap.fix: A clue naming Botticelli, Zephyrus, a scallop shell, or the Uffizi means this exact painting. A clue jumping between several different painters, or calling her “Aphrodite,” means the broader goddess tossup — wait for a clear mention of a single painting before you answer with this one.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Birth of Venus (accept “La Nascita di Venere”; prompt on “Venus”; do not accept “Aphrodite”)
